claims.text: Moderate oxygen partial pressures promote selective oxidation at nanoparticle surfaces under high-temperature catalytic conditions.
Selective surface oxidation triggers elemental segregation because the constituent elements have different oxidation enthalpies.
Reducing environments preserve the homogeneous, near-equiatomic solid-solution structure.
Near-equiatomic CoCrFeNiPd nanoparticles can initially have a homogeneous, disordered solid-solution phase.
Oxide layers and associated elemental segregation develop through atomic-scale rearrangements at nanoparticle surfaces and interfaces.
Oxygen selectively oxidizes the less noble constituents at the nanoparticle surface.
Selective oxidation consumes active metal sites.
Selective oxidation reduces local mixing entropy.
The oxidation-induced reduction in local mixing entropy accelerates surface diffusion.
Accelerated surface diffusion promotes elemental segregation and eventual phase separation.
Oxidizing conditions cause surface segregation to begin at a lower temperature than under reducing conditions.
Oxidizing conditions cause phase separation to begin at a lower temperature than under reducing conditions.
Under reducing conditions, the solid-solution structure is maintained to higher temperatures than under oxidizing conditions.
A reducing or inert baseline atmosphere produces minimal surface oxidation and delayed or absent segregation.
The proposed mechanism applies between 500 K and 1200 K when oxygen partial pressure exceeds a threshold.
The mechanism's applicability under extreme thermoelectric conditions or very low oxygen concentrations is unresolved.
TEM electron-beam exposure may produce secondary effects that complicate interpretation of nanoparticle dynamics.
